title: Why I Don’t Write Much About Large-Scale Teaching Reform and Policy Change https://davestuartjr.com/why-i-dont-write-much-about-large-scale-teaching-reform-and-policy-change/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a reader who asks why the blog focuses on teachers' inner resilience rather than pushing for systemic reform, Dave Stuart Jr. takes the challenge seriously and answers candidly. He names the goal of his work as the long-term flourishing of teachers, on the grounds that flourishing teachers are best for students, and concedes that advocacy for more humane conditions would plausibly serve that goal. His answer is deliberately called weak: with about fifteen free hours a week and little knowledge of how policy is made, he judges that policy work is not where he can contribute, and he will not sacrifice family and community to try. He leaves the door open for readers who feel called to that research and writing.
points: Frames the blog's purpose as promoting teacher flourishing, grounded in Seligman's PERMA model, with the claim that great teachers tend to have great lives.
Admits that structural conditions such as long days and ill-fitting mandated PD harm teachers and that advocacy against them is a reasonable strategy.
Justifies a narrower focus through honest limits of time and knowledge rather than dismissing policy work.
Treats constraint and clarity of purpose as a kind of strength, and invites others to take up humane school reform.
quotes: Right now, I think the goal of my work is to promote the long-term flourishing of teachers, that there might someday be flourishing, professional educators in every school in the world. It’s taken me some time to be comfortable with that because it’s a line that doesn’t mention students at all.
But the thing I can’t escape is that flourishing teachers are best at promoting the long-term flourishing of young people.
Wouldn’t it be smarter for us to advocate against these kinds of conditions? For a version of school that is more humane, more generative of long-term teacher and student flourishing?

Basically, I have only so much time. During the school year, I’ve got about 15 hours per week to do everything not directly related to my classroom — writing, research, emails, management, meetings, and all the things.

There are some great people who devote 80 hours per week to their work in education. In my own life, I’m not inclined to do this as I feel it would be forsaking my wife and children and the community where I work and live.
And I suppose in that acknowledgment of weakness, there is a certain amount of strength, of the kind that come from clarity of purpose.
